claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Holender, 1986 and Holender and Duscherer, 2004.

claims.claim: The subjective threshold approach claims to take consciousness seriously by letting participants indicate whether they experience a stimulus.
claims.source: The core difference between objective and subjective threshold models is that the subjective threshold approach claims to take consciousness seriously by letting the participants in a study indicate on their own terms whether they experience (see) a stimulus at a certain level of intensity (Baars, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baars, 1994.

claims.claim: Participants have well above-chance objective sensitivity for presentation levels at which they claim stimuli are subjectively invisible.
claims.source: Typically, participants have well above-chance objective sensitivity for presentation levels at which they claim that stimuli are 'subjectively' invisible Stein et al., 2021) and regardless of response criterion or bias (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Balsdon and Azzopardi, 2015; Green and Swets, 1966).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stein et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Objective measures align best with a scientific approach to consciousness.
claims.source: Although objective measures seem to align best with a scientific approach to consciousness (replicable, objective, e.g. see Mei et al., 2022; Soto et al., 2019), they do require one to invoke a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that in fact does not exist (Koenderink, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mei et al., 2022 and Soto et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Objective measures require invoking a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that does not exist.
claims.source: Although objective measures seem to align best with a scientific approach to consciousness (replicable, objective, e.g. see Mei et al., 2022; Soto et al., 2019), they do require one to invoke a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that in fact does not exist (Koenderink, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koenderink, 2014.

claims.claim: Cases have been reported in which subjective experience differs even when objective performance is equated.
claims.source: Indeed, cases have been reported in which subjective experience is reported to be different even when objective performance is equated (Fleming et al., 2010a; Hesselmann et al., 2011; Lau and Passingham, 2006; Persaud et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Subjective measures are the measure of choice in paradigms where physical stimulation is kept identical.
claims.source: Furthermore, subjective measures are the measure of choice in paradigms in which physical stimulation is kept identical, which are often introduced to prevent that differences between conscious and unconscious vision can be attributed to physical rather than 'mental' differences (so-called 'threshold' approaches, Sanchez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sanchez et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Subjective measures have been widely criticized for being confounded by effects unrelated to conscious experience.
claims.source: Subjective measures on the other hand have been widely criticized for being confounded by effects that are unrelated to conscious experience, such as non-perceptual biases as well as regression to the mean effects (for critical reviews see Newell and Shanks, 2014; Schmidt, 2015; Shanks, 2017; Soto et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to critical reviews.

claims.claim: Subjective measures have gained considerable popularity in consciousness research over the past 20 years.
claims.source: Nevertheless, subjective measures have gained considerable popularity in consciousness research over the past 20 years (Dehaene et al., 2003; King et al., 2016; King and Dehaene, 2014; Lamy et al., 2009; Michel, 2022; Overgaard et al., 2010; Overgaard et al., 2006; Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004; Salti et al., 2015; Sandberg et al., 2010; Sergent et al., 2005; Sergent and Dehaene, 2004; Soto et al., 2019; Soto et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by numerous citations to studies using subjective measures.

claims.claim: A dominant approach in subjective threshold literature is to sort trials based on observer's responses to calculate average neural activation for 'seen' versus 'unseen' trials.
claims.source: A dominant approach in the subjective threshold literature is to sort trials based on observer's responses to calculate the average neural activation for 'seen' (conscious) versus 'unseen' (unconscious) trials.
claims.evidence: This is presented as an established methodological approach.

claims.claim: Unconscious working memory has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
claims.source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing this phenomenon.

claims.claim: Unconscious error detection has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
claims.source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Charles et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Unconscious arithmetic has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
claims.source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sklar et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Arbitrary criterion placement influences the decision about stimulus absence or presence, even when consciousness of the stimulus itself is not affected.
claims.source: Arbitrary criterion placement influences the decision about stimulus absence or presence, even when consciousness of the stimulus itself is not affected.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a key insight about criterion effects.

claims.claim: Two stimuli that undergo identical sensory processing and result in the same experience might be reported as seen or unseen depending on whether the observer adopts a liberal versus conservative criterion.
claims.source: Thus, two stimuli that undergo identical sensory processing and result in the same experience might either be reported as seen or as unseen, depending on whether the observer adopts a liberal versus a conservative criterion for deciding whether the threshold for a 'stimulus present' decision was reached.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of criterion effects in signal detection theory.

claims.claim: Perceptual decisions may be motivated by non-perceptual information such as payoff matrix or statistical regularities, even when subjective experience is not affected.
claims.source: For example, it is well known that perceptual decisions may be motivated by non-perceptual information, such as the payoff matrix (the perceived utility of certain responses) or by statistical regularities in the environment, even when subjective experience is not affected (Rungratsameetaweemana et al., 2018; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023b; White and Poldrack, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Roughly two thirds of consciousness researchers at ASSC conference answered that payoff-based criterion shifts do not involve changes in conscious perception.
claims.source: Indeed, when a large group of consciousness researchers at the Association of Scientific Studies of Consciousness (ASSC) conference was asked about the relationship between payoff-based criterion shifts and conscious perception, roughly two thirds answered that they did not think that such shifts involve changes in conscious perception (Q2 in Francken et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francken et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory.
claims.source: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Green and Swets, 1966) and has long been hypothesized to underly many – if not all – subjective threshold effects (Eriksen, 1960; Goldiamond, 1958; Peters and Lau, 2015; Phillips, 2021; Phillips, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to signal detection theory and related work.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts have been hypothesized to underlie many or all subjective threshold effects.
claims.source: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Green and Swets, 1966) and has long been hypothesized to underly many – if not all – subjective threshold effects (Eriksen, 1960; Goldiamond, 1958; Peters and Lau, 2015; Phillips, 2021; Phillips, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: In signal detection theory, the relationship between an observer's response and the signal depends on the criterion applied to that signal.
claims.source: In signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966), the relationship between the response (behavior) of an observer and the signal that the observer operates on, depends on the criterion that the observer applies to that signal.
claims.evidence: This is a fundamental principle of signal detection theory, supported by citation.

claims.claim: When the criterion shifts from conservative to liberal, the average signal strength within both seen and unseen response categories decreases.
claims.source: For example, when the response criterion shifts from conservative to liberal, as is shown in the example in Figure 1A, the average signal strength within both the seen and the unseen response category decreases (see leftward diagonal lines from conservative to liberal).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A showing the signal detection theory model.

claims.claim: A more conservative criterion inflates neural measures of both unconscious and conscious processing when compared to a liberal criterion.
claims.source: Somewhat counterintuitively, a more conservative criterion does not have different effects on the neural measure of 'unconscious' processing and on the neural measure of 'conscious' processing. Instead, when the two criteria are positioned symmetrically around the mean of the signal distribution as in the left panels of Figure 1B, a more conservative criterion inflates neural measures of both unconscious and conscious processing when compared to a liberal criterion (see the right panel of Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: This consequence of criterion shifts on effect sizes in neural measures based on post hoc sorted trials has not been highlighted in the consciousness literature.
claims.source: Although this consequence of criterion shifts on effect sizes in neural measures based on post hoc sorted trials is clearly implied by signal detection theory, to our knowledge it has not been highlighted in the consciousness literature.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding in the consciousness literature.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, participants viewed a continuous rapid serial visual presentation of oriented textures while EEG was collected.
claims.source: To investigate this, we analyzed two datasets in which a criterion manipulation was applied to a detection task. In both experiments, participants viewed a continuous rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of oriented textures while EEG was collected (see Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claims.claim: The fifth texture in the sequence either contained a texture-defined square or a homogenous texture without a square.
claims.source: The sequence of textures was always identical, except that the fifth texture either contained a texture-defined square of lines orthogonal to the background orientation (target trials) or a homogenous texture without such a square (no-target trials).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus manipulation in the experiments.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, participants were punished with an aversive tone and monetary deduction for misses in the liberal condition.
claims.source: To manipulate their decision criterion, they were either punished using an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for misses (liberal condition) or an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for false alarms (conservative condition).
claims.evidence: This describes the criterion manipulation method in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, participants were punished with an aversive tone and monetary deduction for false alarms in the conservative condition.
claims.source: To manipulate their decision criterion, they were either punished using an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for misses (liberal condition) or an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for false alarms (conservative condition).
claims.evidence: This describes the criterion manipulation method in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, participants responded using the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS).
claims.source: In a second experiment, we had a different group of participants perform the same task, this time responding using the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS: Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the response method in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The PAS allows observers to indicate the strength of their experience at a fine-grained resolution ranging from 0 'No experience' to 3 'A clear experience'.
claims.source: This scale allows observers to indicate the strength of their experience at a more fine-grained resolution ranging from [0] 'No experience' to [3] 'A clear experience' (PAS experiment, see Figure 2B and Methods for full description of the four response categories).
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the PAS scale.

claims.claim: The underlying assumption of the PAS is that selecting 0 will only occur if trials are truly unseen.
claims.source: The underlying assumption of the PAS is that selecting [0] will only occur if trials are 'truly' unseen, so that unconscious processing is not overestimated, as may happen in dichotomous or other types of scales (Overgaard et al., 2006; Overgaard and Sandberg, 2021; Sandberg et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to papers about the PAS.

claims.claim: The PAS was developed to be impervious to non-perceptual criterion shifts.
claims.source: The PAS was developed to be able to resolve the inability to externally calibrate subjective content, and as such its ultimate goal seems to be to be impervious to non-perceptual criterion shifts.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the stated purpose of the PAS.

claims.claim: The degree to which the PAS is robust to non-perceptual criterion shifts has never been explicitly investigated.
claims.source: However, despite its popularity, the degree to which the PAS is robust to non-perceptual criterion shifts has never been explicitly investigated.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research on this topic.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, observers were explicitly instructed to respond in line with their experience.
claims.source: Here, to counter criterion shifts when using the PAS, we further explicitly instructed observers to respond in line with their experience: 'Even though you receive feedback about the correctness of your responses, it is very important that you keep responding according to what you actually experience, using the Perceptual Awareness Scale. Only press 0 if you are 100% convinced that no square appeared and only press 3 if you are 100% convinced that a square appeared.'
claims.evidence: This describes the instructions given to participants in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, target presentation duration was 40 ms.
claims.source: Aside from response mode and target presentation duration (Experiment 1: 40 ms, Experiment 2: 30 ms), both experiments were virtually identical (see Methods for other minor differences).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail of Experiment 1.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, target presentation duration was 30 ms.
claims.source: Aside from response mode and target presentation duration (Experiment 1: 40 ms, Experiment 2: 30 ms), both experiments were virtually identical (see Methods for other minor differences).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The criterion manipulation resulted in a strong criterion shift in both experiments.
claims.source: Behaviorally, the criterion manipulation (liberal vs conservative) resulted in a strong criterion shift in both experiments, expressed in concomitant increases of both hits (responding 'seen' when a target was presented) and false alarms (responding 'seen' when no target was presented) for liberal when compared to the conservative condition (see left panels of Figure 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: Sensitivity remained largely unchanged between liberal and conservative conditions in both experiments.
claims.source: In contrast, sensitivity – simplified here as the hit rate minus the false alarm rate – remained largely unchanged (right panel of Figure 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, the criterion manipulation exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.84) than on d' (hedges g = 0.30).
claims.source: To quantify the success of the criterion manipulation in Experiment 1, we computed the signal theoretic parameter estimates criterion c (liberal: –0.30, conservative: 0.73) and sensitivity d' (liberal: 2.12, conservative: 2.39). This confirmed that the criterion manipulation in Experiment 1 was successful, and that it exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.84) than on d' (hedges g = 0.30).
claims.evidence: This is based on signal detection theory analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: All levels of the PAS are affected by criterion shifts.
claims.source: In contrast, however, we observed strong criterion shifts on all levels of the PAS, as can be seen from concomitant increases of both hits and false alarms for liberal when compared to the conservative condition (see left panels of Figure 2D), while sensitivity (collapsing PAS1, PAS2, or PAS3 as 'seen' responses) was only slightly higher for conservative compared to liberal (see the right panel of Figure 2D). This shows for the first time, that all levels of the PAS are affected by criterion shifts, questioning the construct validity of the measure (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, the criterion manipulation exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.02) than on d' (hedges g = 0.42).
claims.source: Computing the corresponding signal theoretic estimates for Experiment 2 confirms this result for criterion c (liberal: –0.59, conservative: 0.60) and sensitivity d' (liberal: 1.29, conservative: 1.59). Effect sizes on these measures show that the criterion manipulation in Experiment 2 worked and that it exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.02) than on d' (hedges g = 0.42), just as we observed in Experiment 1.
claims.evidence: This is based on signal detection theory analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: A linear discriminant analytic classifier was trained for each participant to discriminate target from no-target trials based on EEG data.
claims.source: Next, to establish the effect of criterion shifts on neural measures, we turned to classification performance of EEG data as a measure of neural processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2018). First, a linear discriminant analytic (LDA) classifier was trained for each participant using all trials from all sessions (three sessions in Experiment 1, two sessions in Experiment 2) to discriminate target from no-target trials based on EEG data, irrespective of seen/unseen responses and irrespective of the response criterion.
claims.evidence: This describes the neural data analysis method.

claims.claim: A leave-one-person-out cross validated decoding scheme was applied to maximize signal-to-noise ratio.
claims.source: To maximize signal-to-noise ratio, we applied a leave-one-person-out cross validated decoding scheme by using all classifiers from all participants except the participants that was being tested (separately for Experiment 1 and for Experiment 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Classification was performed using occipitoparietal electrodes as these are most sensitive to the stimuli used.
claims.source: We maximized signal-to-noise ratio by performing classification using occipitoparietal electrodes, as these are known to be most sensitive to these stimuli (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Fahrenfort et al., 2008; Fahrenfort et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing electrode sensitivity.

claims.claim: Three local maxima in classification performance occurred at 137, 266, and 430 ms.
claims.source: We subsequently computed the average classification performance across both experiments (see Figure 3A, left panel) and identified three times at which local maxima occurred in this average (137, 266, and 430 ms).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A based on the neural data analysis.

claims.claim: The three peaks in classification performance have highly similar topographic maps of current source density for both experiments.
claims.source: Figure 3A (right panel) shows that these peaks have highly similar topographic maps of current source density, obtained from the forward transformed weights of the training data from the selected peaks for both experiments (Haufe et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A based on topographic analysis.

claims.claim: Classification performance was higher for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2.
claims.source: Note that classification performance was higher for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2, as this experiment had 3 sessions instead of 2, and target stimuli were presented for 40 ms instead of 30 ms (which also resulted in a higher behavioral d' for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of neural decoding results between experiments.

claims.claim: Trial counts were equated between liberal and conservative conditions within each participant to ensure differences could not be explained by disparities in signal-to-noise ratio.
claims.source: To ensure that differences resulting from post hoc sorting could not be explained by differences in signal-to-noise ratio resulting from disparities in trial counts in the testing set, we equated trial counts between the liberal and conservative condition within each participant by randomly selecting the same number of trials from overrepresented cells (for Experiment 1, this was done at the level of 'seen' and 'unseen' responses, for Experiment 2 the trial counts were equated at each of the PAS levels, see methods for details).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological control in the analysis.

claims.claim: A 2 (experiment) × 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment, visibility, criterion, and latency.
claims.source: We then entered these in a large 2 (experiment) × 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA with experiment as a between group factor. The result of this ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment (Exp1 vs Exp2: F1,40 = 38.68, p < 10–6, η²p = 0.49), visibility (seen vs unseen: F1,40 = 204.01, p < 10–16, η²p = 0.84), criterion (liberal vs conservative: F1,40 = 20.98, p < 10–4, η²p = 0.34), and latency (137, 266, and 430 ms: F1.79,80 = 33.72, p < 10–8, η²p = 0.46), see Supplementary file 1a for the full ANOVA.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claims.claim: Post hoc sorting results in higher classification performance for the conservative than for the liberal condition.
claims.source: These data confirm – as was predicted from our simulation – that post hoc sorting results in a large criterion effect, with higher classification performance for the conservative than for the liberal condition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the neural decoding results shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Criterion did not significantly interact with experiment (F1,40 = 1.38, p = 0.25, η²p = 0.03).
claims.source: The consistency of the effect is further supported by the fact that criterion did not significantly interact with experiment (F1,40 = 1.38, p = 0.25, η²p = 0.03).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claims.claim: Criterion interacted with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12).
claims.source: Criterion did interact with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12), and with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1), indicating that criterion effects on neural measures manifested differentially in different visibility levels and at different moments in time.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claims.claim: Criterion interacted with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1).
claims.source: Criterion did interact with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12), and with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1), indicating that criterion effects on neural measures manifested differentially in different visibility levels and at different moments in time.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claims.claim: In both experiments, the criterion effect occurs at long latencies (266 and 430 ms) but not at the short latency of 137 ms.
claims.source: Indeed, in both experiments the criterion effect occurs at long latencies (266 and 430 ms) but not at the short latency of 137 ms, as was established using one-sided t-tests (conservative >liberal) for simple effects in each of the three latencies for each of the two experiments (see Figure 3B, for the complete time courses of these experiments see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: There was a highly significant three-way interaction between criterion, experiment, and visibility (F1,40 = 18.47, p < 10–3, η²p = 0.32).
claims.source: Finally, there was a highly significant three-way interaction between criterion, experiment, and visibility (F1,40 = 18.47, p < 10–3, η²p = 0.32), which we will expound on in much more detail further down below.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claims.claim: Without post hoc sorting, there was no main effect of criterion on classification performance (F1,40 = 1.16, p = 0.29, η²p = 0.03).
claims.source: To test for criterion effects in the absence of post hoc sorting, we then entered these data in a 2 (experiment) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA with experiment as a between group factor (naturally there was no factor visibility because there was no post hoc sorting). As before, the result of this ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment (Exp1 vs Exp2: F1,40 = 28.45, p < 10–5, η²p=0.42), and latency (137, 266, and 430 ms: F1.70,67.95 = 49.95, p < 10–12, η²p = 0.56), but this time there was no main effect of criterion (liberal vs conservative: F1,40 = 1.16, p = 0.29, η²p = 0.03), see Supplementary file 1b for the full ANOVA.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of neural data without post hoc sorting.

claims.claim: The criterion effects observed with post hoc sorting are due to post hoc sorting and not due to general effects of decoding sensitivity in the conservative versus liberal condition.
claims.source: Figure 3C shows the effect of the criterion manipulation separately for the two experiments, with one-sided post hoc t-tests (conservative > liberal) for each of the three latencies. This figure shows that – if anything – the criterion effect is in the opposite direction of the effect observed in Figure 3B, further confirming that the criterion effects in Figure 3B are due to post hoc sorting and not due to general effects of decoding sensitivity in the conservative versus the liberal condition.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of analyses with and without post hoc sorting shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, criterion strongly interacts with visibility (F1,15 = 11.06, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.42).
claims.source: For Experiment 1, we performed a 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA (see Supplementary file 1c for the full ANOVA). This analysis again shows strong main effects of visibility (F1,15 = 81.38, p < 10–6, η²p = 0.84), criterion (F1,15 = 13.89, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.48), and latency (F2,30 = 37.13, p < 10–8, η²p = 0.71), but more importantly, it also shows that criterion strongly interacts with visibility in Experiment 1 (F1,15 = 11.06, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.42).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Experiment 1 data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, criterion effects were only significant in the 'unseen' condition but not in the 'seen' condition.
claims.source: One-sided t-tests for simple effects (conservative > liberal) revealed that the criterion effects were only significant in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4A, left panel), but not in the 'seen' condition (Figure 4A, right panel), and – as established before – that these effects only appear in the late 266/430 ms latencies as opposed to the early 137 ms latency.
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, criterion interacts with visibility (F2.29,41.37 = 2.86, p = 0.06, η²p = 0.10).
claims.source: To investigate the interaction between visibility and criterion in Experiment 2, we performed the same analysis in a 4 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA, this time maintaining the four PAS responses as separate levels in the factor visibility (see Supplementary file 1d for the full ANOVA). Again, this analysis confirmed strong main effects of visibility (F2.37,59.22 = 67.29, p < 10–16, η²p = 0.73), criterion (F1,25 = 10.10, p = 0.004, η²p = 0.29), and latency (F1.89,47.28 = 13.26, p < 10–4, η²p = 0.35), as observed in Experiment 1. Moreover, this experiment-specific ANOVA confirms that here too, criterion interacts with visibility (F2.29,41.37 = 2.86, p = 0.06, η²p = 0.10).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, criterion effects were predominantly in the 'seen' conditions of the PAS (PAS1, PAS2, and PAS3) but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0).
claims.source: Post hoc t-tests for simple effects (conservative > liberal) revealed that in Experiment 2, the criterion effects were predominantly in the 'seen' conditions of the PAS (PAS1, PAS2, and PAS3, see Figure 4B, second, third, and fourth panels), but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0, see Figure 4B, leftmost panel), whereas Experiment 1 showed a significant effect in 'unseen' but not in 'seen' (and again only at late 266 and/or 430 ms latencies).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: When sensitivity is low, a small criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting.
claims.source: First, we manipulated the degree of sensitivity (Figure 4C, D), while keeping the response thresholds for responding 'seen' or 'unseen' the same. When sensitivity is low (Figure 4C, left panels), a small criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4C, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When sensitivity is high, a criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the 'unseen' condition.
claims.source: Conversely, when sensitivity is high (Figure 4D, left panels) the same criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4D, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Under identical signal detection thresholds, a change in sensitivity can have a large differential impact on neural measures in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions.
claims.source: These simulations show that under identical signal detection thresholds, a change in sensitivity (e.g. when showing higher strength stimuli, or when an observer is more attentive), can have a large differential impact on the neural measures in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions, making their interpretation intrinsically problematic.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: When the overall criterion is conservative, a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting.
claims.source: In a second simulation, we looked at the effect of overall criterion shifts (Figure 4E, F), while keeping sensitivity the same. When the overall criterion is conservative (Figure 4E, left panels), a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4E, right panel), whereas when the overall criterion is liberal (Figure 4F, left panels) the same criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4F, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: When the overall criterion is liberal, a criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition.
claims.source: In a second simulation, we looked at the effect of overall criterion shifts (Figure 4E, F), while keeping sensitivity the same. When the overall criterion is conservative (Figure 4E, left panels), a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4E, right panel), whereas when the overall criterion is liberal (Figure 4F, left panels) the same criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4F, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Small criterion shifts can have a differential impact on effect size in neural measures of 'seen' and 'unseen' stimuli depending on whether the overall criterion is liberal or conservative.
claims.source: This shows that small criterion shifts can have a differential impact on the effect size in neural measures of 'seen' and 'unseen' stimuli, even when sensitivity stays the same, depending on whether the overall criterion is liberal or conservative, again making the interpretation of such effects problematic.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts can differentially confound neural measures of conscious or unconscious processing depending on both overall criterion and sensitivity.
claims.source: Thus, criterion shifts can differentially confound neural measures of conscious or unconscious processing, depending both on overall criterion and sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the simulation results.

claims.claim: The direction of criterion influence on neural measures can be counterintuitive, is difficult to predict, and cannot be controlled experimentally.
claims.source: The direction of this influence can be counterintuitive, is difficult to predict, and cannot be controlled experimentally.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation and empirical results.

claims.claim: Experiment 1 has a much higher sensitivity than Experiment 2.
claims.source: Interestingly, Experiment 1 has a much higher sensitivity than Experiment 2 (both in terms of classification accuracy and in terms of behavioral sensitivity, as pointed out before).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of behavioral and neural measures between experiments.

claims.claim: The difference in sensitivity between Experiments 1 and 2 provides a compelling explanation for why Experiment 1 shows the largest effect of criterion shift in the unseen condition while Experiment 2 shows it in the PAS1 condition and up.
claims.source: This provides a compelling explanation for our finding that Experiment 1 (detection) shows the largest effect of the criterion shift in the unseen condition, whereas for Experiment 2 (PAS) the largest effect was observed in the PAS1 condition and up, which is nicely in line with the predictions from our simulation in Figure 4C, D.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the empirical results to the simulation predictions.

claims.claim: Criterion and sensitivity either cannot be controlled in principle or are not controlled in practice.
claims.source: Importantly, these factors either cannot be controlled in principle (criterion) and/or are not controlled in practice (sensitivity), which questions the construct validity of subjective measures under post hoc sorting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for experimental practice.

claims.claim: Post hoc sorting on 'seen' and 'unseen' responses causes neural effect sizes to become stronger under a conservative compared to a liberal response criterion.
claims.source: In this manuscript, we have shown through simulation that post hoc sorting on 'seen' and 'unseen' responses causes neural effect sizes in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions to become stronger under a conservative compared to a liberal response criterion.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts modulated effect size in neural measures of 'unconscious' and/or 'conscious' processing in both experiments.
claims.source: To test this claim empirically, we analyzed data from two experiments in which criterion shifts were induced experimentally (one using a simple detection task, one using the PAS). We found that in both experiments, criterion shifts modulated effect size in neural measures of 'unconscious' (unseen) and/or 'conscious' (seen) processing, and that this happens even though the conservative and liberal condition used the same independent training data (identical classifiers), and even though the trial counts in the test sets were equated for the conservative and liberal condition.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main empirical finding.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing under post hoc sorting.
claims.source: Together, these data show that criterion shifts confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing under post hoc sorting.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the combined simulation and empirical results.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts potentially contaminate studies of unconscious cognition.
claims.source: Such confounds potentially contaminate studies of unconscious cognition (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011) as well as studies that apply post hoc sorting to reveal neural measures of consciousness through a contrastive approach (van Boxtel et al., 2010; Hesselmann et al., 2011; Hesselmann and Malach, 2011; Levinson et al., 2021; Melloni et al., 2011; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Rolke et al., 2001; Salti et al., 2015; Sanchez et al., 2020; Sergent et al., 2005; Stein et al., 2021; van Vugt et al., 2018; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for prior studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The contrast 'seen > unseen' can result in strong or weak differences between conditions depending on the response criterion adopted by observers.
claims.source: Concretely, the contrast 'seen > unseen', used in neuroimaging studies to isolate the neural basis of consciousness, can either result in strong or in weak differences between conditions, depending on the response criterion that was adopted by the observers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for the interpretation of neural contrasts.

claims.claim: Arbitrary criterion placement is intrinsic to decision making.
claims.source: Unfortunately, arbitrary criterion placement is intrinsic to decision making, and is known to be affected by many factors that are not controlled between, or even within experiments.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about decision making.

claims.claim: Context has a large effect on how observers place their criterion.
claims.source: Context is known to have a large effect on how observers place their criterion. For example, the ratio of targets to non-targets (the base-rate), the strength of the target stimulus compared to noise (the signal-to-noise ratio), the utility of certain stimulus–response combinations (the payoff matrix), and even small changes in task instructions are all known to affect the response criterion (Fleming et al., 2010b; Kloosterman et al., 2019; Rakhshan et al., 2020; Supèr et al., 2001; White and Poldrack, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing contextual effects on criterion.

claims.claim: The omnipresence of arbitrary criterion placement due to non-perceptual influences threatens the construct validity of subjective measures in consciousness research.
claims.source: So even if some criterion shifts may have a perceptual origin (Meyerhoff and Scholl, 2018; Witt et al., 2015), the omnipresence of arbitrary criterion placement due to non-perceptual influences (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023a; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023b) threatens the construct validity of subjective measures in consciousness research.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for subjective measures, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts threaten the construct validity of the PAS.
claims.source: Relatedly, criterion shifts also threaten the construct validity of the PAS.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the empirical results of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Experiment 2 shows that all levels of the PAS are sensitive to the criterion manipulation, even when explicitly instructing participants to only respond according to their experience.
claims.source: Experiment 2 shows that all levels of the PAS are sensitive to the criterion manipulation, even when explicitly instructing participants to only respond according to their experience.
claims.evidence: This is based on the behavioral results from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Both payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts result in a bias on first order decisions and affect how second order confidence judgements are distributed.
claims.source: This finding is in line with evidence showing similar effects on related subjective measures, such as confidence judgements. For example, both payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts not only result in a bias on first order decisions, but also affect how second order confidence judgements are distributed (Lebreton et al., 2019; Lebreton et al., 2018; Locke et al., 2020), also see Peters et al., 2017.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on confidence judgments.

claims.claim: Payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts affect confidence scores even when perceptual experience is not affected.
claims.source: Indeed, recent experiments from our lab have confirmed that payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts affect confidence scores even when perceptual experience is not affected (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work from the authors' lab.

claims.claim: Any context influences the criterion in some way.
claims.source: However, proper instruction does not resolve this issue. Any context – experimentally induced or not – influences the criterion in some way, and if there is no way to enforce that the adopted criterion is an unwavering threshold on subjective experience (and nothing else), any subjective measure is potentially prone to confounds of a non-experiental nature.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the fundamental problem with subjective measures.

claims.claim: Without resolving the criterion problem, any experiment remains open to the critique that participants may not have adopted the subjective scale as intended.
claims.source: Without resolving this, any experiment remains open to the critique that the participants in the study may not have adopted the subjective scale as it was intended, for whatever reason.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for experimental validity.

claims.claim: Criterion shifts are well known to occur without experimental manipulations and occur naturally across experiments with different ratios of target to non-targets and different overall levels of visibility.
claims.source: Nevertheless, criterion shifts are well known to also occur without these manipulations and occur naturally across experiments that have different ratios of target to non-targets, different overall levels of visibility and so forth.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about criterion shifts.

claims.claim: The current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice.
claims.source: As such, the current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: There is no such thing as a criterion-free experimental context.
claims.source: Importantly, there is no such thing as a criterion-free experimental context.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a fundamental principle about experimental contexts.

claims.claim: Many dimensions that are not controlled between experiments will have a large effect on the criterion even without manipulating it explicitly.
claims.source: As pointed out in the beginning of this discussion and in our simulations, many dimensions that are not controlled between experiments, will have a large effect on the criterion even without manipulating it explicitly/experimentally.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation and empirical results.

claims.claim: Many view subjective measures as a crucial behavioral marker of the presence or absence of consciousness.
claims.source: Thus, researchers studying consciousness are faced with a difficult conundrum. On the one hand, many view subjective measures as a crucial behavioral marker of the presence or absence of consciousness (Baars, 1994; Dehaene, 2014; Overgaard et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to researchers advocating for subjective measures.

claims.claim: Subjective measures do not reliably measure the construct they intend to measure due to criterion confounds.
claims.source: On the other hand, subjective measures do not reliably measure the construct they intend to measure due to criterion confounds.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study's findings.

claims.claim: Peters and Lau (2015) proposed combining an objective first order judgment with a criterion-free subjective measure by having participants place bets on their objective judgment.
claims.source: A potential way out of this conundrum has been a proposal by Peters and Lau, 2015. They combined an objective, first order judgment with a criterion-free subjective measure by having participants place bets (as proxy for subjective reports) on their objective judgment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters and Lau, 2015.

claims.claim: In the Peters and Lau study, trials consisted of two intervals with only one containing a grating target, and subjects were asked to guess grating orientation for both intervals and place a bet on which judgment is more likely to be correct.
claims.source: Trials consisted of two intervals, only one of them containing a grating target, and subjects were asked to guess grating orientation for both intervals and place a bet on which of these two judgments is deemed as more likely to be correct.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of Peters and Lau's study.

claims.claim: Peters and Lau argued that above-chance objective performance in the absence of subjective insight measured in a criterion-free way would reflect unconscious perception.
claims.source: They argued that above-chance objective performance in the absence of subjective insight measured in this criterion-free way would reflect unconscious perception.
claims.evidence: This describes the theoretical argument of Peters and Lau.

claims.claim: Saving the construct validity of subjective measures requires solving the criterion problem.
claims.source: Without making any final judgment on this matter, we point out that saving the construct validity of subjective measures requires one to solve the criterion problem (Morgan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about what is needed to address the validity issues, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Without a properly experimentally defined procedure for solving the criterion problem, the construct validity of subjective measures will remain under threat.
claims.source: Without a properly experimentally defined procedure for doing so, their construct validity will remain under threat.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for future research.

claims.claim: Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate neural correlates of both 'unconscious' and 'conscious' conditions.
claims.source: Summarizing, aside from the effect of the criterion on behavioral responses themselves, we show both empirically and in simulation that post hoc trial sorting of neural data on subjective measures can have unintuitive consequences depending on the experimental context (i.e. depending on the criterion that participants adopt). Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate estimates neural correlates of both 'unconscious' (unseen) and 'conscious' (seen) conditions, whereas experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding do the reverse.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations and empirical data.

claims.claim: Experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding will underestimate neural correlates of both 'unconscious' and 'conscious' conditions.
claims.source: Summarizing, aside from the effect of the criterion on behavioral responses themselves, we show both empirically and in simulation that post hoc trial sorting of neural data on subjective measures can have unintuitive consequences depending on the experimental context (i.e. depending on the criterion that participants adopt). Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate estimates neural correlates of both 'unconscious' (unseen) and 'conscious' (seen) conditions, whereas experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding do the reverse.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations and empirical data.

results.result: Signal detection theory simulations demonstrate that conservative criterion placement inflates neural measures of both conscious and unconscious processing compared to liberal criterion placement. When the criterion shifts from conservative to liberal, average signal strength decreases in both 'seen' and 'unseen' response categories, leading to counterintuitive effects on neural effect sizes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are well-supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1. The signal detection theory framework clearly demonstrates the predicted effects, and the authors correctly note this consequence has not been previously highlighted in consciousness literature despite being implied by signal detection theory. The simulation methodology is sound and the conclusions follow logically from the model.

results.result: Two EEG experiments were conducted using rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of oriented textures. Experiment 1 (N=16) used a detection task with payoff-based criterion manipulation (40ms target duration), while Experiment 2 (N=26) used the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS) with explicit instructions to respond according to experience (30ms target duration).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C54 describe the experimental design and are well-documented in the Methods section and Figure 2. The experimental procedures are clearly described with appropriate detail about stimulus parameters, task instructions, and criterion manipulations. The designs are appropriate for testing the hypotheses.

results.result: The criterion manipulation successfully induced strong criterion shifts in both experiments, with concomitant increases in hits and false alarms under liberal versus conservative conditions, while sensitivity (d') remained largely unchanged. Effect sizes confirmed much larger effects on criterion (Exp1: g=2.84; Exp2: g=2.02) than on sensitivity (Exp1: g=0.30; Exp2: g=0.42).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C59 are strongly supported by the behavioral data in Figure 2C-D and signal detection theory analyses. The manipulation checks demonstrate successful criterion shifts with minimal sensitivity changes, which is essential for isolating criterion effects. The effect size calculations appropriately quantify the manipulation success.

results.result: All levels of the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS) were affected by criterion shifts, showing concomitant increases in both hits and false alarms across PAS0-PAS3 responses. This occurred despite explicit instructions to respond only according to experience, demonstrating that the PAS does not guard against criterion confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C6, C100 are well-supported by the behavioral data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 2D. The finding that all PAS levels show criterion effects is novel and important. However, the authors acknowledge (and critics have noted) that the specific instructions and feedback used may differ from standard PAS implementation, which could limit generalizability. Despite this caveat, the result challenges assumptions about PAS robustness.

results.result: EEG classification analysis used leave-one-person-out cross-validation with LDA classifiers trained on occipitoparietal electrodes to discriminate target from no-target trials. Three classification performance peaks were identified at 137, 266, and 430ms with similar topographic patterns across experiments. Trial counts were equated between conditions to control for signal-to-noise differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 describe the neural analysis methodology, which is appropriate and well-controlled. The leave-one-person-out cross-validation maximizes training data while ensuring independence. Trial count equation is a critical control. The identification of three temporal peaks with consistent topography across experiments (Figure 3A) provides confidence in the reliability of the neural measures.

results.result: A 2×2×2×3 ANOVA revealed significant main effects of criterion on neural classification performance after post hoc sorting, with higher performance for conservative versus liberal conditions. Criterion effects occurred at late latencies (266, 430ms) but not early (137ms), and interacted significantly with visibility and latency but not experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 report the primary statistical results supporting criterion effects on neural measures. The ANOVA design is appropriate, and the results clearly demonstrate the predicted criterion effects. The temporal specificity (late but not early latencies) and the three-way interaction with experiment and visibility are important nuances. Statistical reporting is complete with F-values, p-values, and effect sizes.

results.result: Without post hoc sorting on responses, there was no main effect of criterion on classification performance (F1,40=1.16, p=0.29), and if anything the effect was in the opposite direction. This confirms that criterion effects observed with post hoc sorting are due to the sorting procedure itself, not general differences in neural sensitivity between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 describe a critical control analysis shown in Figure 3C. This control effectively rules out the alternative explanation that conservative conditions simply have better neural decoding overall. The absence of criterion effects without post hoc sorting, combined with opposite-direction trends, strongly supports the interpretation that post hoc sorting creates the observed confounds.

results.result: In Experiment 1 (detection task), criterion strongly interacted with visibility (F1,15=11.06, p<0.01), with significant criterion effects only in the 'unseen' condition at late latencies (266, 430ms) but not in the 'seen' condition or at early latency (137ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by the experiment-specific ANOVA and post-hoc tests shown in Figure 4A. The finding that criterion effects are specific to the 'unseen' condition in the high-sensitivity detection task is important for understanding how experimental context modulates criterion confounds. Statistical evidence is appropriate.

results.result: In Experiment 2 (PAS task), criterion interacted with visibility (F2.29,41.37=2.86, p=0.06), with criterion effects predominantly in the 'seen' conditions (PAS1-3) at late latencies but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0), showing an opposite pattern to Experiment 1.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by the experiment-specific ANOVA and post-hoc tests shown in Figure 4B. The opposite pattern from Experiment 1 (effects in 'seen' rather than 'unseen') is a key finding that motivates the follow-up simulations. The marginally significant interaction (p=0.06) is appropriately interpreted in context of the clear post-hoc effects.

results.result: Follow-up simulations manipulating sensitivity while keeping response thresholds constant showed that when sensitivity is low, criterion shifts have larger effects on 'seen' neural measures, whereas when sensitivity is high, criterion shifts have larger effects on 'unseen' neural measures. This demonstrates that sensitivity changes can differentially impact neural measures in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are well-supported by the simulation results in Figure 4C-D. These simulations provide a mechanistic explanation for the differential effects observed between Experiments 1 and 2. The simulations are appropriately designed to isolate the effect of sensitivity, and the results clearly demonstrate the predicted patterns.

results.result: Follow-up simulations manipulating overall criterion placement while keeping sensitivity constant showed that when the overall criterion is conservative, criterion shifts have larger effects on 'seen' neural measures, whereas when the overall criterion is liberal, criterion shifts have larger effects on 'unseen' neural measures.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are well-supported by the simulation results in Figure 4E-F. These simulations demonstrate an additional factor (overall criterion placement) that modulates where criterion confounds manifest. The simulations appropriately isolate this factor and demonstrate clear differential effects on 'seen' versus 'unseen' conditions.

results.result: Criterion shifts differentially confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing depending on both overall criterion and sensitivity. The direction of influence is counterintuitive and difficult to predict. The higher sensitivity in Experiment 1 versus Experiment 2 explains why criterion effects appeared in 'unseen' versus 'seen' conditions respectively, consistent with simulation predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 synthesize the simulation and empirical findings. The explanation linking differential sensitivity between experiments to the observed pattern of results is compelling and well-supported by the simulations in Figure 4C-D. The conclusion that these factors cannot be controlled in principle (criterion) or practice (sensitivity) is justified, though somewhat pessimistic about potential solutions.

results.result: Post hoc sorting on 'seen' and 'unseen' responses causes neural effect sizes to become stronger under conservative compared to liberal response criteria. This was demonstrated through both simulations and empirical data from two experiments, confirming that criterion shifts confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing under post hoc sorting.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93, C4-C5 represent the core findings of the manuscript. These are strongly supported by converging evidence from simulations (Figure 1) and two independent experiments with different response scales (Figures 2-4). The methodological controls (trial count equating, independent training data, control analyses without post hoc sorting) strengthen confidence in the conclusions.

results.result: Criterion placement threatens the construct validity of neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing. These confounds potentially contaminate existing studies using post hoc sorting approaches, and the omnipresence of arbitrary criterion placement due to non-perceptual influences means subjective measures do not reliably measure the construct they intend to measure.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C94-C95, C98, C110 represent the main conclusions about implications for the field. These are well-supported by the empirical findings, though they represent strong interpretive claims. The authors appropriately cite numerous studies that could be affected. The conclusion about construct validity is justified given the demonstrated confounds, though some may debate whether this completely invalidates subjective measures or whether solutions exist.

results.result: Arbitrary criterion placement is intrinsic to decision making and affected by many uncontrolled factors including base-rate, signal-to-noise ratio, payoff matrix, and task instructions. There is no criterion-free experimental context, and criterion shifts occur naturally across experiments even without explicit manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C103, C105, C107-C108 are supported by established signal detection theory principles and cited empirical work. These claims provide important context for why the demonstrated confounds are problematic - criterion cannot be eliminated or fully controlled. The claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature.

results.result: Criterion shifts threaten the construct validity of the PAS specifically. Similar effects have been shown for confidence judgments, where payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts affect confidence distributions even when perceptual experience is not affected. Without resolving the criterion problem, experiments remain open to critique about whether participants adopted the subjective scale as intended.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C101-C102, C104 extend the findings to the PAS and related subjective measures. The empirical evidence from Experiment 2 supports the PAS-specific claims, though with caveats about the specific implementation. The citations to work on confidence judgments (C101-C102) appropriately contextualize the findings within broader issues with subjective measures.

results.result: Peters and Lau (2015) proposed a potential solution combining objective first-order judgments with criterion-free subjective measures using betting paradigms. However, saving the construct validity of subjective measures requires solving the criterion problem through properly defined experimental procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 discuss potential solutions but remain somewhat speculative. The authors appropriately describe the Peters and Lau approach but express uncertainty about whether it truly solves the problem. The claim that solving the criterion problem is necessary (C114-C115) is more of a recommendation than an empirically tested result. These represent important discussion points but lack the empirical support of the main findings.

results.result: Post hoc sorting based on 'seen'/'unseen' judgments is a hallmark approach in consciousness research, but cognitive and response biases strongly affect criterion placement. While the criterion problem has been known since signal detection theory and hypothesized to underlie subjective threshold effects, the specific effect of criterion placement on neural measures under post hoc sorting has never been explicitly investigated.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C29, C37-C38, C42 establish the background and novelty of the work. These are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. The claim of novelty (C3, C42) appears justified - while criterion effects are well-known, their specific consequences for post hoc sorted neural measures had not been systematically investigated. This establishes the importance of the current work.

results.result: The introduction provides historical context about consciousness research, including the rejection of introspectionism and behaviorism, the development of the contrastive approach, debates between objective and subjective threshold approaches, and the rise of post hoc sorting methods that have been used to propose phenomena like unconscious working memory, error detection, and arithmetic.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C32 provide historical and theoretical background. These are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature and represent accurate characterizations of the field's development. While these are primarily review/background claims rather than novel findings, they are important for contextualizing the current work and are accurately presented.

results.result: Arbitrary criterion placement influences decisions about stimulus presence/absence even when consciousness is not affected. Two stimuli undergoing identical processing may be reported differently depending on criterion. Perceptual decisions can be motivated by non-perceptual information like payoff or base-rate, and most consciousness researchers believe such criterion shifts do not involve changes in conscious perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36, C39 establish key theoretical principles about criterion effects. These are well-supported by signal detection theory (C39) and empirical citations (C35-C36). The survey of consciousness researchers (C36) provides useful context about field consensus. These claims appropriately set up the motivation for investigating criterion effects on neural measures.

results.result: The current experiments can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice. Many researchers view subjective measures as crucial for consciousness research, yet experimental contexts inducing conservative responses overestimate neural correlates of both conscious and unconscious conditions, while liberal contexts do the reverse.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C109, C116-C117 provide important framing and summary of implications. The characterization as a 'caricature' (C106) appropriately acknowledges that the experimental manipulation is more extreme than natural variation, while still being relevant to actual practice. The summary of main findings (C116-C117) accurately reflects the empirical results.

results.result: Conservative criterion placement inflates neural effect sizes in both conscious and unconscious processing, while liberal criterion placement reduces them. This counterintuitive finding was demonstrated through simulations (C40, C41) and confirmed empirically in EEG decoding analyses (C68), showing higher classification performance for conservative compared to liberal conditions after post hoc sorting.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states the 'evidence supporting this criticism is compelling, based on simulations and decoding analysis of EEG data.' The anonymous reviewer confirms 'findings consistently indicated that adopting a more conservative response criterion could enhance neural decoding performance, whether in conscious or unconscious states.' No concerns are raised about this central result.

results.result: The Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS) does not guard against criterion confounds. All levels of the PAS (0-3) were affected by criterion shifts in Experiment 2, even when participants were explicitly instructed to respond according to their experience.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly acknowledges this finding, noting the study included 'a more detailed four-level response (ranging from 0 for no experience to 3 for a clear experience)' and that criterion effects were observed across all levels. The editor's statement that the evidence is 'compelling' encompasses this result. No reviewer challenges this finding about the PAS.

results.result: The experimental context (sensitivity and overall criterion placement) determines whether criterion shifts have larger confounding effects on neural measures of conscious versus unconscious processing. Simulations showed that low sensitivity produces larger effects in 'seen' conditions while high sensitivity produces larger effects in 'unseen' conditions, explaining differences between Experiments 1 and 2.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly confirms this finding, stating 'adopting a more conservative response criterion could enhance neural decoding performance, whether in conscious or unconscious states, depending on the sensitivity or overall response threshold.' This demonstrates reviewer acceptance of the context-dependent nature of criterion effects. No concerns are raised about these simulation results or their interpretation.

results.result: The criterion manipulation successfully induced strong criterion shifts in both experiments while leaving sensitivity largely unchanged. In Experiment 1, the manipulation had a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.84) than on d' (hedges g = 0.30), with similar results in Experiment 2 (criterion: g = 2.02; d': g = 0.42).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly validates the manipulation, stating 'it is evident that response criterion can influence the results' and noting the findings were 'observed in simulated data as well as in two experiments that manipulated the subject response criterion to be either more liberal or more conservative.' The successful dissociation between criterion and sensitivity effects is implicitly accepted through the reviewer's focus on criterion effects.

results.result: Without post hoc sorting, there was no main effect of criterion on classification performance, confirming that the criterion effects observed with post hoc sorting are due to the sorting procedure itself and not to general differences in neural decoding sensitivity between liberal and conservative conditions.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer implicitly accepts this control analysis by stating 'when comparing the neural decoding performance of Target versus NonTarget with or without post-hoc sorting based on subject reports, it is evident that response criterion can influence the results.' This acknowledgment of the contrast between conditions with and without post hoc sorting indicates acceptance of this methodological control.

results.result: Criterion effects on neural measures occur at late latencies (266 and 430 ms) but not at early latency (137 ms). In Experiment 1, effects were significant only in the 'unseen' condition, while in Experiment 2, effects were predominantly in 'seen' conditions (PAS1-3) but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer does not explicitly discuss the temporal dynamics or the differential effects across visibility conditions, but accepts the overall finding that criterion affects neural measures. The editor's statement that the evidence is 'compelling' based on 'decoding analysis of EEG data' encompasses these temporal and condition-specific patterns. No concerns are raised about these specific patterns.

results.result: Criterion placement threatens the construct validity of neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing, potentially contaminating many prior studies using post hoc sorting approaches. Subjective measures do not reliably measure consciousness due to criterion confounds.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly endorses this conclusion, stating the study 'provides a critical challenge to a great many studies of the neural correlates of consciousness that were based on post hoc sorting of reported awareness experience.' The anonymous reviewer's acceptance of the empirical findings implicitly supports this validity concern. The editor notes the results 'will be of interest not only to psychologists and neuroscientists but also to philosophers,' indicating recognition of the broad implications.

results.result: Trial counts were equated between liberal and conservative conditions within each participant to ensure differences in neural decoding could not be explained by disparities in signal-to-noise ratio due to unequal trial numbers.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly addresses this methodological concern, noting 'The uneven distribution of trails for Target (75%) and NonTarget (25%) was identified as a potential weakness in the initial review of this study. Nevertheless, we support the authors' assertion that their analysis methodology validates comparing liberal and conservative approaches.' This demonstrates reviewer acceptance of the trial equating procedure as adequate.
